rows.jobs: About 50 direct jobs per typical building; roughly 100-200 direct jobs at county level (independent research). Industry studies citing ~1,300 jobs per 100 MW include modeled indirect and induced effects and are not comparable to direct counts.
rows.water: Design-dependent: most Virginia facilities use about the same or less water than a large office building; evaporative designs use far more.
rows.power: ~100 MW continuous, orders of magnitude above any comparably sized warehouse or most factories. This is the defining impact and the reason for utility and grid review.
rows.truckTraffic: Very low in operations (small headcount, occasional deliveries); heavy truck traffic concentrates in the 12-36 month construction period. Qualitative: no published operational traffic study exists.
rows.taxRevenue: Highest per acre of the three where equipment is taxable: data centers supply 38% of Loudoun County's general fund on ~4% of commercial parcels. Ohio modeling put a 250,000 sq ft data center at $84M annual peak taxes vs $62M for comparable manufacturing.
rows.notes: Low jobs, low operating traffic, very high power demand, high per-acre tax yield where personal property taxes apply.

rows.jobs: Varies enormously: general warehousing employs relatively few per square foot, while e-commerce fulfillment centers employ hundreds to over a thousand.
rows.water: Low: domestic and fire protection use only, no process cooling load.
rows.power: Low single-digit MW typical for lighting, conveyors, and HVAC (qualitative).
rows.truckTraffic: Measured: 0.22-0.60 daily vehicle trips per 1,000 sq ft (PennDOT / ITE), roughly 190-520 daily trips for an 870,000 sq ft building with a large share of heavy trucks, continuing for the life of the facility.
rows.taxRevenue: Lower per acre: value sits in the building shell and land, with far less taxable equipment than a data center.
rows.notes: More jobs per building than a data center in the fulfillment case, dramatically more permanent truck traffic, minimal power and water.

rows.jobs: About 250 direct jobs in Ohio modeling, roughly 3x a same-size data center's direct count.
rows.water: Highly process-dependent: food processing and chemicals can exceed data center use; light assembly uses little. No single figure is defensible.
rows.power: Process-dependent, typically 5-30+ MW, almost always well below a hyperscale data center (qualitative).
rows.truckTraffic: Moderate to high: inbound materials and outbound product generate sustained truck volumes (qualitative).
rows.taxRevenue: $62M modeled annual peak taxes vs $84M for the comparable data center in the Ohio analysis.
rows.notes: The classic tradeoff: manufacturing brings roughly 3x the direct jobs; the data center brings more tax revenue in the Ohio model.

comparison.defensibilityNote: These comparisons contextualize orders of magnitude; they are not equivalent-confidence data. The Ohio data-center-vs-manufacturing figures are modeled projections summarized by a law firm serving the industry, and they count multiplier effects that independent research suggests are often overstated. Warehouse employment spans a 10x range by subtype, so no single jobs number is defensible. Warehouse and factory power and water figures are qualitative because no tier-1 per-facility source was located. Tax comparisons depend entirely on state tax structure. The traffic row mixes measured warehouse rates with inferred data center rates.

receives.detail: Local property tax on buildings plus, in states that tax it, large business equipment tax revenue (up to 38% of the county budget in the extreme Loudoun case).
Substations, water lines, and fiber routes built or funded by the project, which can serve wider growth.
About 50 direct permanent jobs per building at solid wages, plus a large multi-year construction workforce.
Hundreds to thousands of trades workers spending locally for 1-5+ years of phased building.
Negotiated benefits where communities ask: fire equipment and staffing, workforce training funds, scholarships, broadband extensions.
Documented cases of developer-funded stations, trucks, and training that improved response times district-wide.

accepts.detail: Hundreds of acres of buildings and pavement, effectively permanent, often on former farmland.
Load comparable to tens of thousands of homes, with grid upgrade and rate-structure consequences that depend on state rules.
12-36 months per building of truck traffic, dust, and noise; years for phased campuses.
Continuous cooling hum and periodic generator testing, manageable by design and enforceable limits, painful where those are absent.
Design-dependent water consumption, generator emissions within permitted limits, stormwater and habitat impacts of a large campus.
Warehouse-scale architecture, security fencing, and lighting where fields or woods used to be.

futureTech.summary: In production for AI racks (22% of surveyed operators) and effectively required for the highest-density systems; 75% of the installed base still uses air cooling.
Microsoft's new-build standard since late 2024: closed-loop chip-level cooling that eliminates evaporative water use at the cost of modestly higher electricity (company-reported).
Operating in Europe (Amazon Dublin heating council buildings since 2022; Meta Odense feeding Danish district heat); rare in the US because district heating networks are scarce.
Bloom Energy reports 1.3+ GW deployed and a 1 GW agreement with AEP for AI data centers; gas-fed, so cleaner locally than diesel but not zero-carbon (company-reported).
Google has contracted 1 GW of demand-response capacity with five US utilities, shifting AI workloads during grid peaks; contracted capacity, limited public curtailment data so far (company-reported).
Three Mile Island Unit 1 restart (835 MW, Microsoft) targets mid-2027; the restructured 1,920 MW Talen-AWS Susquehanna deal runs through 2042 after FERC rejected the behind-the-meter version.
Commercially available for high-density niches; adoption remains a small fraction of the market compared with direct-to-chip.
Google and Xcel plan a 300 MW / 30 GWh 100-hour battery for a Minnesota data center; in regulatory review, not operating.
No SMR powers any data center today. Google-Kairos targets around 2030; Amazon-X-energy targets 320 MW initially. All dates are developer targets, not regulatory certainties.
